To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the participants in our ethnographic study of outdoor physical activity in Wales reported that they enjoyed the visual and haptic dimensions of their outdoor leisure activities, and that they experienced a range of ‘intense embodied’ sensations.
the participants in this study experienced intense embodiment in the outdoors.
the sensory dimensions of outdoor exercise embodiment can be understood in terms of a complex and dynamic interplay of visual, haptic, and other sensory dimensions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people ‘sense the outdoors’ through their bodies and with the embodied meanings that they make of this.
the ways in which participants ‘make sense of the senses’, in the context of a range of outdoor activities, and how they ‘sensate the outdoors’.
the ‘sensuous geographies’ of embodied physical activity, and with the ‘sensualities’ of outdoor exercise embodiment in particular.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the visual and haptic sensory engagement of outdoor exercise is a highly complex phenomenon, and that this complexity is not only a product of the physical and social environment, but is also shaped by individual and collective embodied experience and by the cultural and social context.
the visual and the tactile senses are central to the experience of outdoor exercise embodiment, but that this is not always the case.
the sensory dimension of embodiment is a complex and multi-layered phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

participants were ‘sensory tourists’ who were ‘sensing the outdoors’ through their embodied experiences of outdoor leisure activities, and that the Programme provided them with the opportunity to ‘re-sense the outdoors’ in ways that were often transformative.
participants’ experiences of the Programme are mediated through a sensory engagement with the outdoors, which is a complex and dynamic process.

the Programme participants’ embodied engagement with the natural environment was highly sensory and that this was a significant factor in shaping the experience of physical activity, and of the natural environment itself.
The main takeaway from our work is that
participants were able to engage in embodied outdoor physical activities that were both ‘natural’ and ‘social’.
the embodied experiences of participants in organised outdoor activities are highly complex and multi-sensory, and are not reducible to the visual.

the sensory dimension of outdoor physical activity is a significant and often overlooked aspect of exercise embodiment, and that a sensory phenomenology can offer important insights into the lived experience of physical activities in outdoor leisure environments.
